conditions.unmeasured: figures downstream of a constant nobody has measured are absent rather than estimated
conditions.what_an_interval_here_is: a statement about this model's declared inputs, and nothing about whether the model has the right structure (ch14, ch19)

produced_by.sampler: sizing.mc — inverse transform, Iman-Conover rank correlation

correlations.because: The unhappy one. A busier system is usually a slower one per request - caches miss more, locks are held longer, the garbage collector runs while somebody is waiting. Treating the two as independent understates the tail of every figure in this model, and it understates it exactly when the tier is busiest.

summary.description:
The smallest model in the book, and the one that is not a chain of multiplications. Part II is about ceilings: the places where a system stops behaving like the product of its inputs and starts behaving like something else. This model has two of them.
The first is the queueing knee. Waiting time is not proportional to load; it is proportional to load divided by what is left of the machine, which means it is flat and then vertical. The second is what happens when you add machines to fix the first: sharing costs something, and past a point it costs more than the machine brings.
Nothing here names a product. The shapes are properties of queues and of shared state, and they turn up in a database, a message broker, a web tier and a storage cluster alike.

achievable_throughput.label: throughput the tier can actually reach
achievable_throughput.note: The universal scalability law. One node's throughput times the count, divided by what contention and crosstalk take back. With crosstalk at zero it is Amdahl's ceiling; with both at zero it is the straight line nobody has ever measured.

provenance.source: ch03 - requests per second at the busy hour. Triangular because this is an engineer's min/likely/max and claiming more shape than that would be invention.

busy_nodes.label: nodes busy on average
busy_nodes.note: Arrival rate times service demand. It is a count of machines doing work, it has nothing to do with how many you own, and it is the numerator of every utilisation figure below.

concurrency.label: requests in the system
concurrency.note: Little's law, and the only relationship in Part II that is always true: the number of requests in a system is the rate they arrive at times how long each one stays. No distribution assumed, no queue discipline assumed, nothing assumed except that the system is in a steady state. ch05 is about what that buys and what it does not.

contention.label: contention
contention.note: The fraction of the work that cannot be done in parallel: a lock, a single writer, a shared queue. It costs a fixed share of every machine you add, so it flattens the scaling curve and never bends it downwards.

provenance.source: ch07 - fitted from two measurements, where two exist

ceiling.because: The same queueing margin as above, applied to the capacity the tier actually has rather than to the capacity its parts would have had alone. Where the two ceilings disagree, this is the one that is about the system you own (ch07).

crosstalk.label: crosstalk
crosstalk.note: The cost of machines having to agree with each other, which grows with the number of pairs rather than the number of machines. This is the term that makes the curve turn over: past some count, the next machine costs more in agreement than it brings in work.

provenance.source: ch07 - fitted, and the hardest of the two to fit

headroom_to_peak.label: fraction of the peak already built

provenance.source: the sizing decision for this tier

one_node.label: one node
one_node.note: as elsewhere: a conversion has to be a node before the division means anything

optimism.label: how much the queueing view understated it

peak_nodes.label: where adding nodes stops helping
peak_nodes.note: Where the scalability curve turns over, from the two coefficients alone: the square root of one-minus-contention over crosstalk. Past it, throughput falls. It is a property of the software, not of the budget, and no amount of money moves it.

ceiling.because: Not a capacity limit: a tier at ninety per cent of capacity has not run out of anything, it has a queue in front of it. The margin is large because the cost of crossing it is paid in latency by every request, not in a failure somebody gets paged for (ch06).

residence_time.label: residence time
residence_time.note: Service time divided by the fraction of the tier that is idle. That single division is ch06's whole subject: it is nearly flat while there is slack and nearly vertical when there is not, and nothing about the arithmetic warns you which side you are on.

ceiling.because: At half, one machine in two is paying for the other's coordination. There is no failure and nothing gets paged; the tier simply costs twice what its work is worth, and it will go on doing so until somebody looks. A budget is the only thing this ceiling protects, which is why the margin is the loosest in the book and why it is still worth declaring (ch07).

scaling_loss.label: fraction of the tier doing nothing useful

service_demand.label: service demand per request
service_demand.note:
Node-seconds of work one request costs, which is not the same thing as how long a request takes. A request that occupies one node for six milliseconds has a service demand of six milliseconds whether it returns in six milliseconds or in six seconds - the difference between those two is queueing, and this model is about that difference.
It is declared as an assumption and it should be a `rig` measurement (ch03). Nobody has taken one, and the model says so here rather than in a footnote.

provenance.source: stated workload characteristic; belongs on the rig and has not been measured

service_seconds.label: service time
service_seconds.note: service demand with the machine divided out: how long one request would take alone

provenance.source: throughput of one node alone, as quoted

utilisation_cap.label: utilisation the model will admit to
utilisation_cap.note: A modelling choice, stated rather than hidden. The waiting-time formula below divides by what is left of the tier, so at a utilisation of one it divides by zero and returns infinity. Infinity is not a prediction. Past this point the formula has stopped describing a queue and started describing an arithmetic accident, so the model clamps and the ceiling reports that it is over.

provenance.source: where this model stops being about queues (ch06)

utilisation_including_coordination.label: utilisation, counting coordination
utilisation_including_coordination.note:
The same tier's utilisation, worked out from what it can actually deliver rather than from what one node could deliver alone. It is higher than the row above, always, and the gap is the work the machines are doing on each other's behalf.
Reading those two rows next to each other is ch07's whole argument. The queueing view of Part II is not wrong; it is optimistic, and it is optimistic by a factor nobody notices until they measure the tier at two sizes and find the second one disappointing.

scenario.because: The tier as declared. Every figure Part II quotes comes from here unless it says otherwise.
